source.title: Double Descent, Ensemble Emergence, and Large Model Averaging in High-Dimensional Multimodel Prediction
source.authors: Keyi Chen; Dandan Jiang; Xin-Yu Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and examines double-descent risk in nested linear-model prediction and model averaging, rather than reproducing the original deep-network settings.
record.gate_note: The paper's own asymptotic risk results and explicit descriptions of the risk curves are included. Comparisons of LaMA's predictive accuracy with AIC, BIC, MMA, JMA, and other methods are not rows because they do not measure the double-descent behavior itself. The study does not test deep networks or training epochs.
record.test_reason: The paper derives exact asymptotic out-of-sample risk for nested least-squares model averaging (min-norm OLS candidates) using random matrix theory. It then plots that risk against the number of candidates M (fixed n) and the sample size n (fixed M). This gives the paper's own results on model-wise and sample-wise double descent in a non-deep-network setting (linear model ensembles), so it bears on V3, V4 and V6. It does not reproduce the deep-network recipe.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that simple (equal or random) weighting of nested high-dimensional models inherits a double-descent risk peak driven by variance explosion near the interpolation boundary, though reduced relative to a single model. Variance-based 'high-risk, low-weight' allocation can completely suppress the peak, giving a globally flat risk surface they call ensemble emergence. They propose LaMA, which replaces in-sample variance with asymptotic out-of-sample variance and adds a variance-weighted ℓ2 penalty, and report the lowest or competitive prediction error in simulations and two small real datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses random-matrix asymptotics for nested linear least-squares models and model averaging, with risk curves over model dimension and sample size; it does not use deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The risk profile changes with weight allocation (equal, random, or variance-penalized) and with whether the singular kq=n submodel is retained or excluded. The reported sweeps also vary M at fixed n and n at fixed M.

fits_no_version.finding: Weighting candidates by reciprocal asymptotic variance removes the double-descent peak entirely, giving a flat risk surface ('ensemble emergence'), even with the singular kq=n model retained.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In model averaging, variance-aware weight allocation (not tuned ridge regularization) suppresses the interpolation-threshold peak.

record.problems: The double-descent claims are supported primarily by asymptotic theory and plotted risk curves, with few plotted values tabulated. The evidence concerns nested linear models under stated random-matrix assumptions, not deep networks. The random-weight result is only summarized in the supplied text, with details deferred to supplementary material.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. LaMA-versus-baseline simulation and real-data performance results were left out because they compare prediction methods rather than report the double-descent curve itself.

untested.parts: All of it: no deep networks or model-size sweeps of trained networks.
All of it: no training-time or epoch axis.
Deep-network sample-size sweeps. Only nested linear model averaging (asymptotic) is examined.
Model classes beyond nested min-norm least-squares and their averages. No finite-sample deep or kernel models.
All of it: no single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
No label-noise sweep (σ² and SNR fixed in the risk plots). No triple or multiple peaks. No optimally tuned ridge or other conventional regularization.
All of it: no effective-parameter recounting.

missing.what: Simulated in-sample vs out-of-sample loss against M under equal weights (θj=j^-0.5, p=1000). Out-of-sample loss rises to a peak around the interpolation boundary then decreases, while in-sample loss falls monotonically. This is the only non-asymptotic double-descent curve in the paper.
Bias and variance components over n at fixed M=100. Variance peaks as n approaches model dimensions and vanishes once n>M; bias declines steadily.

record.verdict_notes: Most double-descent evidence is deterministic asymptotic limits (Theorem 3.2) plotted at n=100 or M=100 with SNR=1. The only simulated loss curve is Figure 1, which no row records. R1 restates Hastie et al.'s single-model result and should not be a row. The LaMA comparisons (Figures 6-9, Tables 1-2) are method-performance results, correctly excluded. The x-axis 'M' is the number of nested candidates, which equals the largest candidate's dimension (kq=q), so it acts as a capacity axis. Tranche changed to T3: this is a new setting (linear model ensembles) rather than a different method on the original deep-network question.

versions.untested_parts: Risk over training epochs or training time.
No deep-network sample-size sweep; the result is for nested linear-model averaging.
Only nested linear-model prediction and its averaging strategies are examined, not a broad range of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.

The paper does not test multiple or triple peaks, an explicit label-noise sweep to establish the cause of the peak, or optimally tuned regularization. Its peak-suppression result uses variance-based weighting.
No re-counting of complexity using an effective number of parameters.

rows.subject: single linear model
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed asymptotic out-of-sample risk as model dimension varies relative to sample size.
rows.value: For cq<1 risk increases monotonically; for cq>1 the risk includes a decreasing noise-variance term proportional to 1/(cq−1), yielding the second descent beyond the interpolation boundary.
rows.note: The text says the correctly specified single-model case does not show the usual first descent below the boundary because its approximation bias is zero.
rows.check: This is a cited result, not the study's own. The single correctly specified linear-model risk limit is quoted from Hastie et al. [3] (Proposition 3.1 and the following text). Drop it or mark it as background.

rows.subject: equally weighted model averaging
rows.size_stated: nested candidate dimensions kq=q; n varies
rows.operation_detail: Examined asymptotic risk as M and n vary with equal weights and the singular submodel retained.
rows.measure: out-of-sample risk and its variance near the interpolation boundary
rows.baseline: single-model risk is plotted as a comparator
rows.value: The out-of-sample variance diverges as cq approaches 1; the ensemble risk explodes for M≥n and the M>n region cannot be displayed.
rows.note: The singular retained-model setting exhibits the boundary surge, but the text does not display a subsequent descent in this case.
rows.check: With the kq=n submodel retained, the variance diverges and risk is unbounded for M≥n. That shows the variance-driven peak (V6). The second descent cannot be displayed, so for V4 this row is cannot_determine and should not carry V4.

rows.subject: equally weighted model averaging
rows.size_stated: nested candidate dimensions kq=q; fixed n=100
rows.operation_detail: Examined asymptotic risk as the maximum candidate dimension M increases, excluding the singular submodel.
rows.value: Risk initially declines for M<n, peaks near M=n, and descends again for M>n.
rows.note: The stated curve is for equally weighted model averaging with the singular submodel excluded.
rows.check: Correct. Add that the text says the ensemble peak is 'reduced but still present' relative to the single model. The values are asymptotic limits plotted in Figure 3(b), not tabulated.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2.1, Figure 3(b), and the model-ensemble discussion; Figure 2 supplies the shared signal settings.

rows.subject: equally weighted model averaging
rows.size_stated: fixed M=100; nested candidate dimensions kq=q
rows.operation_detail: Examined asymptotic risk as sample size n increases.
rows.value: As n approaches candidate-model dimensions, instability raises risk to a peak; after n exceeds M, bias and variance decline.
rows.note: The text describes a range in which increasing sample size raises risk before the later decline.
rows.check: Correct. In the n<M region, risk rises as n approaches the candidate dimensions (Figure 3(c)), so more data raises risk there.

source_check.correct: Baseline: asymptotic risk of the largest individual candidate model, shown alongside model averaging; no numerical baseline value is tabulated.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, Equation (11); Figure 3(c) and caption; Section 3.2.1 sample-wise discussion.
source_check.problem: The baseline is recorded as not stated, but Figure 3(c) explicitly includes the single-model comparator.

rows.subject: variance-penalized model averaging
rows.size_stated: nested candidate dimensions kq=q; fixed n=100
rows.operation_detail: Examined risk as M increases using weights proportional to reciprocal asymptotic model variance.
rows.value: The model-averaging risk surface is described as globally flattened, with a smooth trend through M/n≈1 rather than a localized risk surge.
rows.note: This is strategic variance-based weight allocation, not a test of optimally tuned conventional regularization.
rows.check: State should be absent, not observed. Under variance-penalized weights (Eq. 12) the ensemble risk shows no peak or second descent near M/n≈1; the surface is 'globally flattened'. This weighting is not tuned regularization, so the row should not count as V6 evidence (see fits_no_version).

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2.2, Equation (12), Figure 5(b), and discussion immediately following Figure 5.
